title: Subset Sum Count
statement:
A chef has `weights`, the weights of several ingredients (all positive). A **selection** is any choice of ingredients, picked by position, so two ingredients with the same weight at different positions are different choices. The empty selection is allowed.

Count how many selections have a total weight of exactly `target`.

examples.explanation: Either ingredient alone works, and they are counted separately.

hints.nudge: For each ingredient you have exactly two choices. What does each choice do to the remaining target?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: take it or leave it, recursing on the rest, and stop early when you can no longer succeed.
hints.pseudocode:
count(i, remaining):
  if remaining < 0: return 0
  if i == n: return 1 if remaining == 0 else 0
  return count(i + 1, remaining - weights[i]) + count(i + 1, remaining)

answer = count(0, target)
hints.walkthrough: Every selection is a yes/no decision per ingredient, so there are 2^n selections. You can write a recursive function count(i, remaining): if i is past the last ingredient, the selection is valid only if remaining is exactly 0. Otherwise add the ways when you take ingredient i (remaining - weights[i]) and the ways when you skip it. Because all weights are positive, you can prune: once remaining goes below 0, stop. With n up to 15 this is fast enough (at most 32768 selections).
